name: Mehmed II
info: Mehmed II, known as Mehmed the Conqueror (1432–1481), was Ottoman sultan in 1444–1446 and from 1451 to 1481, who took Constantinople in 1453, ending the Byzantine Empire, and rebuilt it as his imperial capital.

facts.born: 30 March 1432 at Edirne, then the Ottoman capital; son of Sultan Murad II and of Hüma Hatun, a slave of uncertain origin
facts.died: 3 May 1481, aged forty-nine, after falling ill at Maltepe at the start of a new campaign; the historian Colin Heywood sees substantial circumstantial evidence of poisoning, possibly at the behest of his son Bayezid; buried in his türbe near the Fatih Mosque
facts.role: Ottoman sultan from August 1444 to September 1446 and from February 1451 to May 1481; governor of Amasya as a boy and of Manisa from 1446 to 1451; after 1453 claimed the title caesar of Rome (Qayser-i Rûm)
facts.known: the conquest of Constantinople in 1453; the end of the Byzantine Empire and of its last states in the Morea and Trebizond; the conquests of Serbia, Bosnia and Anatolia's beyliks; rebuilding and repopulating Istanbul; codifying law in the kanunname; legalising royal fratricide; his library and patronage of Italian artists

t: Made sultan at twelve and set aside two years later, Mehmed returned to the throne in 1451 and at twenty-one took Constantinople after a fifty-seven-day siege, ending the Byzantine Empire.

His thirty years of war added Serbia, the Morea, Trebizond, Bosnia, Albania and the Anatolian beyliks to the empire, at the cost of mass captivity, executions and deportations, and he made Istanbul a thriving capital again.

He centralised government under officials of devshirme background, codified law and legalised the killing of a new sultan's brothers, and he is remembered as a hero in Turkey and, in the Christian world of his day, as a bloodthirsty tyrant.
dyk: To get past the boom chain across the Golden Horn in 1453, Mehmed had about eighty galleys carried overland around the Genoese colony of Galata on a road of wood little over a mile long.
ev: Born at Edirne, the son of Sultan Murad II and Hüma Hatun
Made sultan at twelve when Murad II abdicates; Murad returns to command the army and wins at Varna
Takes Constantinople after a fifty-seven-day siege and moves the Ottoman capital there
Fails to take Belgrade from John Hunyadi and is wounded fighting in person
Takes Trebizond, absorbing the last vestige of Byzantine rule after the Morea
Defeats Uzun Hasan of the Aq Qoyunlu at the Battle of Otlukbeli
The Treaty of Constantinople ends the long war with Venice, which cedes Shkodra and Negroponte
Falls ill at Maltepe at the start of a new campaign and dies

sections.early:
Mehmed was born on 30 March 1432 at Edirne, then the Ottoman capital, the son of Sultan Murad II and of Hüma Hatun, a slave of uncertain origin. At eleven he was sent to govern Amasya with two advisers, as Ottoman custom required, and his father sent teachers with him. His Islamic education shaped his outlook; he followed the approach of his mentor Molla Gürâni, and the sheikh Akshamsaddin impressed on him from a young age the duty of conquering Constantinople. He also showed an early interest in Classical history and European art: his school books carry sketches of ancient coins and portraits in European style, and he reportedly had tutors in Greek and Latin who read him Laertius, Livy and Herodotus.

After making peace with Hungary on 12 June 1444, Murad abdicated in favour of his twelve-year-old son. When a crusade led by John Hunyadi broke the truce that September, Murad led the Ottoman army to victory at Varna on 10 November 1444. Chronicles of the 17th century have Mehmed summoning his father with the words "If you are the sultan, come and lead your armies", but Halil Inalcik holds that it was Çandarlı Halil Pasha who brought Murad back. In 1446 Murad returned to the throne, and Mehmed, keeping the title of sultan, served as governor of Manisa until his father's death in 1451.
sections.rise:
On becoming sultan again in 1451, Mehmed first campaigned against İbrahim II of Karaman, who had stirred revolts, while the Byzantines threatened to release the Ottoman claimant Orhan. He then strengthened the navy and prepared to attack Constantinople. Facing the fortress his great-grandfather Bayezid I had built on the Asian shore of the Bosphorus, he built Rumelihisarı on the European side, took control of the strait and levied a toll on passing ships; a Venetian vessel that ignored the signal to stop was sunk, its surviving sailors beheaded and its captain impaled as a warning.

In early April 1453 he laid siege to the city with an army of between 80,000 and 200,000 men, an artillery train of over seventy large pieces, including the great bombard designed by Orban, and a fleet of 320 vessels. The walls held at first, and a boom chain closed the harbour of the Golden Horn, so on 22 April he had about eighty galleys dragged overland around Galata into the Golden Horn, stretching the defenders along a longer line of walls. Constantinople fell on 29 May after a fifty-seven-day siege. Mehmed, then twenty-one, rode to the Hagia Sophia, ordered it protected and had it made a mosque, and he moved the Ottoman capital from Adrianople to the conquered city.
sections.deeds:
After the conquest Mehmed claimed the title caesar of Rome, a claim the scholar George of Trebizond supported and the Orthodox Church accepted but the Catholic Church and Western Europe did not. Year after year he campaigned. Serbia fell in stages from 1454 to the capture of Smederevo on 20 June 1459. The Morea fell in 1460, its capital Mistra on 29 May, and Trebizond surrendered on 15 August 1461. Bosnia was conquered in 1463, Karaman and Konya taken in 1466, and the Aq Qoyunlu of Uzun Hasan defeated at Otlukbeli in 1473. In 1475 his forces took Kaffa and the Genoese towns of the Crimea and made the Crimean khans tributary princes, and a long war with Venice from 1463 brought him Negroponte in 1470.

At home he rebuilt Constantinople's walls and built a citadel, a hospital, barracks, a gun foundry, mosques including the Fatih Mosque with its eight madrasas, and Topkapı Palace. He ordered Muslims, Christians and Jews to resettle the city, and prisoners of war and deported people were sent there from across the empire; a survey of 1478 counted 16,324 households and an estimated 80,000 people. He restored the Orthodox Patriarchate on 6 January 1454 under Gennadius Scholarius and appointed a grand rabbi. He centralised government under officials of devshirme background, made the religious scholars salaried officials, and between 1477 and 1481 issued a kanunname setting out the duties and salaries of the chief officials.
sections.opponents:
Mehmed's wars met hard resistance. John Hunyadi drove him from Belgrade in 1456, where he was wounded after personally killing three enemy soldiers. Vlad III Dracula of Wallachia refused tribute in 1459, had the Ottoman envoys killed by nailing their turbans to their heads and impaled the force of Hamza Pasha; in 1462 Vlad nearly reached Mehmed in a night attack before the Ottomans took Târgoviște and set up his brother Radu. Skanderbeg held Albania against him until his death in 1468. In 1475 Stephen the Great of Moldavia destroyed an Ottoman army at Vaslui, with Ottoman losses beyond 40,000 according to Venetian and Polish records.

The conquests were violent. The Serbian campaign of 1454 took fifty thousand prisoners, and the captured Serbian voivode Nikola Skobaljić was impaled; in Bosnia Mehmed executed King Stephen Tomašević and his uncle Radivoj; his commander Turahanoğlu Ömer Bey laid 2,000 Wallachian heads at his feet. He formally legalised fratricide, declaring that whichever son took the throne might kill his brothers "for the common benefit of the people", and later sultans executed their brothers and all their male descendants. Franz Babinger writes that the Christian world and part of his subjects regarded him as a bloodthirsty tyrant. His interest in Christian art and relics worried traditionalists, and his son Bayezid accused him of "not believing in Muhammad", though Gülru Necipoğlu notes that sources in Islamic languages do not support such a view of his irreligion.
sections.last:
In his last years Mehmed pressed the war in the west. He personally led the siege of Shkodra in 1478–79, and under the Treaty of Constantinople of 1479 Venice ceded Shkodra, territory on the Dalmatian coast, Negroponte and Lemnos, paid an indemnity of 100,000 ducats and agreed to a yearly tribute of around 10,000 ducats for trading rights in the Black Sea. In 1480 an army under Gedik Ahmed Pasha invaded Italy and captured Otranto, leaving a garrison of 800 infantry and 500 cavalry; so soon after the fall of Constantinople, there was fear that Rome would suffer the same fate, and plans were made to evacuate the Pope and the citizens.

In 1481 Mehmed marched out with the army, planning campaigns against Rhodes and southern Italy, though some historians think his goal was the Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt and the caliphate. On reaching Maltepe he fell ill, and he died some days later, on 3 May 1481, aged forty-nine. Colin Heywood finds substantial circumstantial evidence that he was poisoned, possibly at the behest of his eldest son and successor Bayezid. He was buried in his türbe near the Fatih Mosque. Europe rejoiced: church bells were rung, and Venice proclaimed "The Great Eagle is dead!" Quarrels over the succession, in which Bayezid II fought his half-brother Cem, possibly kept reinforcements from Otranto, which was retaken in 1481. Bayezid sold his father's art collection.
sections.legacy:
Mehmed's thirty-year reign expanded the Ottoman Empire to include Constantinople, the Turkish states of Asia Minor, Bosnia, Serbia and Albania, and Constantinople remained the Turkish capital until the 1920s; fifty years later it was again the largest city in Europe. The historian Neşri wrote that "Sultan Mehmed created all of Istanbul". He is recognised as the first sultan to codify criminal and constitutional law, and so established the classical image of the autocratic Ottoman sultan. Older scholarship credited him with creating the millet system, a claim more recent scholarship considers exaggerated, and the story that he founded the Armenian Patriarchate is a legend.

He gathered Italian artists, humanists and Greek scholars at his court, called Gentile Bellini from Venice to paint his portrait, and built a library of over 8,000 manuscripts in Persian, Ottoman Turkish, Arabic, Latin and Greek; he also wrote poetry under the name Avni. Historians read this patronage as diplomacy with Italian states and as a claim to legitimacy, presenting him as a new Alexander. He left an imposing reputation in both the Islamic and the Christian worlds. In modern Turkey and parts of the Muslim world he is considered a hero: Istanbul's Fatih district, the Fatih Mosque and the Fatih Sultan Mehmet Bridge bear his name, and his picture was on the 1,000 lira note from 1986 to 1992. Rossini made him the subject of the opera Maometto II in 1820.

summary: Mehmed II took Constantinople in 1453, ended the Byzantine Empire and spent three decades extending Ottoman rule over the Balkans and Anatolia, with mass captivity, executions and deportations along the way. He rebuilt Istanbul as a thriving capital, centralised the state and codified its law, and he is remembered both as a national hero and as a tyrant.
